content: Red Ribbon Week is a national initiative in the United States aimed at raising awareness and educating the public about the dangers associated with drug and alcohol use. This event takes place annually during the last week of October, during which students across the country commit to living a drugand alcohol-free lifestyle. Red Ribbon Week is recognized as the most extensive and widely known drug prevention campaign in the United States. The National Family Partnership, which oversees the coordination of Red Ribbon activities on a national scale, estimates that over 80 million Americans participate in events associated with this initiative. The first Red Ribbon Celebration was organized in 1986 by a group of parents who were deeply concerned about the devastating effects of alcohol and drug abuse. The event was created in memory of Enrique Kiki Camarena, a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent who was kidnapped and murdered while investigating drug trafficking operations. His death became a symbol of the fight against drug abuse and trafficking, and the movement gained support from the U.S. Congress. During Red Ribbon Week, many schoolchildren are given red ribbons to wear, often featuring slogans or mottos promoting a drug-free lifestyle. Nancy Reagan, the former First Lady of the United States, is credited with conceptualizing and implementing the idea of Red Ribbon Week as part of her broader efforts to combat drug abuse.
